name: Hemingway Bridge
summary: Ending a work session at a point where you know exactly what comes next, so that resuming the work later is easy.
explanation:
The Hemingway Bridge is the practice of stopping work before you are completely done, at a point where you know what the next step is, and leaving yourself a note about it. The name comes from Ernest Hemingway, who said he always stopped writing when he knew what would happen next, so he could start easily the next day. Tiago Forte popularized the term in Building a Second Brain.

## How It Works

At the end of a session, instead of pushing until you are exhausted or stuck, you:
- Stop at a point where the next step is clear.
- Write down what you were doing, the next step, open questions, and any ideas you have for the continuation.
- Leave the relevant materials where you will find them.

The next session starts by crossing the bridge: reading the note and continuing from there rather than from a blank page.

## Why It Works

- **Ovsiankina Effect**: An intentionally unfinished task keeps a pull to resume it. Stopping mid-task uses that pull instead of fighting it.
- **Shorter resumption lag**: The note preserves the mental context that would otherwise decay, so you get back to full speed faster.
- **Lower starting friction**: Knowing the next action removes the hardest part of starting.
- **Background processing**: Your mind keeps working on the open question between sessions, which often produces new ideas.
- **Sustainable pace**: You stop while you still have energy, so the next session doesn't start from depletion.

## Practical Tips

- End writing sessions mid-paragraph or mid-section with the next sentence or idea noted.
- In code, leave a failing test or a TODO describing the next change.
- Use the last five minutes of the day for a shutdown ritual that includes writing your bridges.
- Keep the bridge note inside the project note so it is the first thing you see when you come back.
